problem: The trap ends with 'that is why the tape, not the tool, set the pace of an NC shop.' This reverses the chapter's own argument, and the worked example: the reader is idle 99 % of the time because the cutter is slow, so the tool sets the pace and the tape does not. A student reading this will learn the opposite of the correct conclusion.
fix: End the bullet with: '...waiting for a slow cutter, and that is why the tool, not the tape, set the pace of an NC shop.'

problem: Section 1 says the classic NC chain has four parts: tape reader, MCU, axis drives and a feedback device (if fitted). Q1's answer gives tape reader, MCU, axis drives and 'the slide with its leadscrew', and then adds the feedback device as an extra. The text and the model answer list different four parts.
fix: Use one list in both places, e.g. Q1 answer: 'Tape reader, machine control unit (MCU), axis drives and the feedback device that reports slide position. On a simple open-loop machine the leadscrew and slide replace the feedback device.'

problem: The step says 'idle percentage = idle time ÷ total cycle time', but the denominator used is 25 s, which is only the machining time. The cycle is reading plus machining = 0.2 + 25 = 25.2 s, so by the stated formula the answer is 24.8 ÷ 25.2 = 98.4 %, not 99.2 %. Q3 has the same slip (19.8 ÷ 20.2 = 98.0 %, not 99.0 %).
fix: Either say 'idle time ÷ machining time' and keep 99.2 %, or keep 'total cycle time' and compute 24.8 ÷ 25.2 × 100 = 98.4 % (Q3: 19.8 ÷ 20.2 × 100 = 98.0 %). State which definition is used.

where: Section 2, paragraph after the bullet list
problem: 'In hard-wired NC each one would have needed new hardware, so none of them existed' contradicts the earlier statement in Section 1 that a canned cycle in hard-wired NC 'needed new boards'. It also overstates the case: simple fixed cycles and tool offsets did exist on some hard-wired controls, wired in as hardware.
fix: Write: 'In hard-wired NC each one had to be built in hardware, so a control offered only the few features its boards were wired for, and any new one meant new boards.'

problem: The instruction 'State which one you mean.' sits inside the definition text, and the two definitions (Direct … and Distributed …) run together with no line break, so the reader sees a single dense block.
fix: Move the instruction out, then give each meaning its own line: 'DNC carries two meanings and they are often mixed. Always say which one you mean.' followed by two separate bullets for the direct and the distributed meaning.

problem: 'the wrong revision is not loaded from a operator's pen drive' — wrong article, and the phrasing is clumsy.
fix: '…so the wrong revision is not loaded from an operator's pen drive.'
